s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an alternative form of {L:Βόες<SDBG:Βόες:000000>}[a] ({D:93.78})

s.dp: Linear Movement › Throw, Hurl
s.d: (derivative of {L:βάλλω<SDBG:βάλλω:000000>}[a] ‘to throw,’ {D:15.215}) the distance which one would normally throw some object
s.g: a (stone’s) throw; the distance one might throw

s.dp: Maritime Activities
s.d: to use a rope with a lead weight attached to it in order to measure the depth of water
s.g: to take soundings; to heave the lead; to drop a plummet

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: watery mud, with an additional feature of filth and uncleanness

s.dp: Spacial Orientations › North, South, East, West
s.c: In most languages east and west are related to the rising or setting sun, although in some languages there may be some local geographical feature which serves as a marker of direction, for example, the location of a particular mountain, the ocean, or a river. For north, some languages employ ‘to the left of the rising sun,’ that is to say, the direction is oriented in terms of the left hand of a person facing toward the rising sun. Similarly, south would be ‘to the right of the rising sun.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to cause animals to eat, particularly pasturing animals
s.g: to feed; to cause to eat
s.c: It is possible to interpret βόσκω in ⟦John 21:15|John 21:15⟧ as meaning ‘to tend’ or ‘to take care of,’ especially since βόσκω occurs in a figurative context referring to people. Such an interpretation may be classified in Domain 35 Help, Care For Subdomain D Care For, Take Care Of, as a figurative meaning. However, it seems more likely that βόσκω in ⟦John 21:15|John 21:15⟧ should be understood as an instance of figurative usage, and as such it may also be interpreted as βόσκω ‘to take care of,’ LN 44.1.

s.dp: Animal Husbandry, Fishing
s.d: to herd animals so as to provide them with adequate pasture and to take care of what other needs may be involved
s.g: to take care of; to herd; to look after
s.c: For another interpretation of βόσκω in ⟦John 21:15|John 21:15⟧, see βόσκω LN 23.10.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: eating by animals
s.c: In some languages a distinction is made in terms relating to eating by animals on the basis of the type of food involved, for example, animals which graze on grass in contrast with those who eat refuse, roots, acorns, etc. An additional distinction is sometimes made in the case of animals which are largely meat-eating in contrast with those that are predominantly plant-eating.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the father of Balaam
s.c: Βοσόρ is the reading in most NT manuscripts for Βεώρ (⟦Numbers 22:5|Numbers 22:5⟧); see LN 93.74. Βοσύρ is an incidental variant spelling (⟦2 Peter 2:15|2 Peter 2:15⟧, apparatus)

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: any of the smaller green plants (in Hellenistic Greek often used in contexts referring to plants as fodder for animals)
s.c: βοτάνη is more generic in meaning than χόρτος, LN 3.15.

s.dp: Plants › Fruit Parts of Plants
s.d: the small round fruit, sweet and juicy, of a creeping plant that develops a woody stem when it matures; Vitis vinifera; symbol of blessing, prosperity, and happiness
s.c: Some scholars have contended that βότρυς means primarily a bunch of grapes, while σταφυλή designates individual grapes. In ⟦Revelation 14:18|Revelation 14:18⟧ this difference might seem plausible, but there is scarcely any evidence for such a distinction, since both words may signify grapes as well as bunches of grapes.|In some languages it is necessary to borrow a term for ‘grapes’ from a dominant language and then employ some kind of classifier, for example, ‘fruit called grapes.’ In other languages grapes may be known as ‘wine fruit,’ since wine may be more widely known than a term for grapes.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: a councilor as a member of the Sanhedrin (see {D:11.80})
s.g: a member of the Sanhedrin; a member of the council

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: to think, with the purpose of planning or deciding on a course of action
s.g: to purpose; to plan; to intend
s.c: In a number of languages there are two quite distinct sets of terms for planning depending upon the purpose involved in such planning. If the planning is constructive, either for oneself or someone else, one set of terms is likely to be used, while if the planning is harmful (usually against someone else), another set of terms would be used.|This meaning is also found as a variant reading: Οἱ δὲ ἀκούσαντες διεπρίοντο καὶ ἐβούλοντο ἀνελεῖν αὐτούς ‘but when they heard this they were furious, for they were planning to put them to death’ ⟦Acts 5:33|Acts 5:33⟧ (apparatus).

s.dp: Think › To Think, Thought
s.d: to think over carefully in an attempt to make a decision
s.g: to think about carefully; to deliberate

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: (derivative of {L:βούλομαι<SDBG:βούλομαι:000001>}[b] and βουλεύομαι[a] ‘to purpose, to plan, to intend,’ {D:30.56}) that which has been purposed and planned

s.dp: Communication › Advise
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to put a plan) to suggest a plan of action

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire, Want, Wish
s.d: (derivative of {L:βούλομαι<SDBG:βούλομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to desire,’ {D:25.3}) that which is desired, with the implication of accompanying planning and will

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: (derivative of {L:βούλομαι<SDBG:βούλομαι:000001>}[b] and {L:βουλεύομαι<SDBG:βουλεύομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to purpose, to plan, to intend,’ {D:30.56}) that which has been purposed and planned

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Desire, Want, Wish
s.d: to desire to have or experience something, with the implication of some reasoned planning or will to accomplish the goal
s.g: to desire; to want; to will

s.dp: Think › To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
s.d: to think, with the purpose of planning or deciding on a course of action
s.g: to purpose; to plan; to intend
s.c: In a number of languages there are two quite distinct sets of terms for planning depending upon the purpose involved in such planning. If the planning is constructive, either for oneself or someone else, one set of terms is likely to be used, while if the planning is harmful (usually against someone else), another set of terms would be used.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Elevated Land Formations
s.d: a relatively low elevated land formation, in contrast with {L:ὄρος<SDBG:ὄρος:000000>} ‘mountain’ ({D:1.46}), which refers to something higher

s.dp: Animals
s.d: general word for individual cattle; may be male (bull or ox) or female (cow); plural: cattle
s.c: In most contexts βοῦς (masc. gender) would seem to refer to an ox (in contrast with ταῦρος ‘bull,’ LN 4.16). In the plural form βοῦς may be translated simply as a collective ‘cattle.’|Though in a number of languages a very special distinction is made between ‘bulls’ and ‘oxen’ (or ‘steers’), no such marked difference occurs in NT usage, and there appears to be no need of introducing any artificial distinction in particular passages.

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Give
s.d: a gift received as a prize or reward as the result of having won in a competition
s.c: In some contexts βραβεῖον refers not to a physical prize or reward but to a spiritual benefit, as in ⟦Philippians 3:14|Philippians 3:14⟧ (τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ‘the prize which is God’s call through Jesus Christ to the life above’).

s.dp: Control, Rule › Control, Restrain
s.d: to control the activity of someone, based presumably upon correct judgment and decision
s.c: In a number of languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘the peace of Christ’ as ‘controlling.’ In some instances one may translate this expression in ⟦Colossians 3:15|Colossians 3:15⟧ as ‘the peace that Christ provides should show you what you should think.’

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: (derivative of {L:βραδύς<SDBG:βραδύς:000000>} ‘slow,’ {D:67.123}) to extend a period of time, with the implication of slowness and/or delay

s.dp: Maritime Activities
s.d: to move slowly by boat

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: pertaining to an extended period of time, with the implication of being slow to do something

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: (derivative of {L:βραδύς<SDBG:βραδύς:000000>} ‘slow,’ {D:67.123}) extending of a period of time, with the implication of slowness and/or delay

s.dp: Power, Force
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of βραχίων ‘arm,’ not occurring in the NT) power as an expression of the activity of a person or supernatural being{N:001}
s.c: In some languages there is no abstract term for ‘power.’ The equivalent of doing something by the power of someone is ‘someone makes it possible to do’ or, in a figurative sense, ‘someone gives strength to do.’

s.dp: Power, Force
s.d: (an idiom, literally: exalted arm, or: lifted up arm) great power, with the implication of an exalted quality
s.g: great power; exalted power; marvelous power

s.dp: Quantity › Many, Few [Countables]
s.d: a relatively small number of objects or events, probably implying less than expected
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of a small or limited number of objects is expressed by a negative attribution to an expression of large quantity, so that ‘few’ becomes ‘not many.’ For another interpretation of διὰ βραχέων in ⟦Hebrews 13:22|Hebrews 13:22⟧, see LN 67.106.

s.dp: Quantity › Much, Little [Masses, Collectives, Extensions]
s.d: a relatively small quantity or extent, probably implying less than expected
s.c: For βραχύ τι in ⟦Hebrews 2:7|Hebrews 2:7⟧, see LN 78.43.

s.dp: Degree › About, Approximately, Almost, Hardly [Approximate Degree]
s.d: a degree of indefinite approximation
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 2:7|Hebrews 2:7⟧ (a quotation from Psalm LN 8.6) the expression βραχύ τι as a lexical unit refers to rank. However, ⟦Hebrews 2:8|Hebrews 2:8⟧ suggests that the writer of Hebrews probably interpreted βραχύ as meaning a small quantity (see LN 59.14) and as referring to time in the sense of ‘a little (while).’ For this interpretation of τι, see LN 92.12.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time{N:001}
s.g: a little while; for a little while; a short time; brief; briefly
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 13:22|Hebrews 13:22⟧ the phrase διὰ βραχέων may refer to the act of sending the communication or the amount of time required to receive the communication, that is to say, to read the communication or to hear it read. For another interpretation of διὰ βραχέων in ⟦Hebrews 13:22|Hebrews 13:22⟧, see LN 59.4.

s.dp: People › Children
s.d: a very small child, even one still unborn
s.c: In a number of languages one must make a clear distinction between a baby after its birth and one before birth, that is, a fetus. Hence, in such languages the term employed in ⟦Luke 1:41|Luke 1:41⟧ must be quite different from the term used in ⟦Luke 2:12|Luke 2:12⟧.

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: the period of time when one is very young{N:001}
s.g: childhood (probably implying a time when a child is still nursing); infancy

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Rain
s.d: rain, whether light or torrential
s.c: Though most languages have a general term for rain, the event of raining is more frequently referred to by a verb rather than by a noun, since rain is something which takes place and is not regarded as a thing or mass, unless, of course, one is referring to the water which comes down as rain, that is to say, ‘rain water’ (see LN 2.10). In some languages the event of raining is generally expressed idiomatically as ‘God is urinating.’ This might appear unduly crude and anthropomorphic, but to the speakers of such a language the expression is often quite acceptable and has no undesirable connotations.|Though in English one may use an impersonal subject with the verb ‘to rain,’ for example, ‘it is raining,’ many languages require some kind of personal agent, for example, ‘God is raining,’ or an impersonal agent such as ‘the sky is raining’ or ‘the clouds are raining.’

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Rain
s.d: to cause rain to fall
s.g: to send rain; to cause it to rain
s.c: In a number of languages one cannot say literally ‘to send rain,’ for this would seem to imply that someone was carrying the rain to some destination. It may be more appropriate, therefore, to speak of ‘causing rain to fall’ or ‘causing rain to come down.’ It may be necessary, however, in some languages to indicate whether the occurrence of rain is for the detriment or the benefit of persons involved, and therefore it may be necessary to say in some instances ‘to cause rain to come down upon for the benefit of’; otherwise the reader might infer that the rain was some kind of punishment.

s.dp: Features of Objects › Wet, Dry
s.d: to make something wet or moist
s.g: to wet; to make wet; to moisten
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made in the use of terms which imply different quantities of moisture, and one must make certain that the choice of a term in ⟦Luke 7:38|Luke 7:38⟧ is in keeping with this context of crying and moistening by means of tears.

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Thunder and Lightning
s.d: the loud sound that accompanies a flash of lightning
s.c: See ἀστραπή lightning (LN 14.16) for further discussion.

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Rain
s.d: rain, whether light or torrential
s.c: Though most languages have a general term for rain, the event of raining is more frequently referred to by a verb rather than by a noun, since rain is something which takes place and is not regarded as a thing or mass, unless, of course, one is referring to the water which comes down as rain, that is to say, ‘rain water’ (see LN 2.10). In some languages the event of raining is generally expressed idiomatically as ‘God is urinating.’ This might appear unduly crude and anthropomorphic, but to the speakers of such a language the expression is often quite acceptable and has no undesirable connotations.|Though in English one may use an impersonal subject with the verb ‘to rain,’ for example, ‘it is raining,’ many languages require some kind of personal agent, for example, ‘God is raining,’ or an impersonal agent such as ‘the sky is raining’ or ‘the clouds are raining.’

s.dp: Control, Rule › Control, Restrain
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to throw a bridle on) to place restrictions upon someone’s behavior
s.g: to restrict; to control; to impose restrictions
s.c: It may, however, be important in some languages to express more clearly the intent involved, and therefore one might wish to translate this clause in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:35|1 Corinthians 7:35⟧ as ‘my purpose is not to try to control you’ or ‘… to tell you just what you must do.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking
s.d: the grinding or the gnashing of the teeth, whether involuntary as in the case of certain illnesses, or as an expression of an emotion such as anger or of pain and suffering
s.g: grinding of teeth; gnashing of teeth
s.c: Though it is possible to interpret βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων as an idiom denoting suffering, it is probably better to understand this in a some what more literal sense (especially in view of biblical views current at that time concerning the next world). It may be important, however, to suggest the significance of this symbolic action, namely, ‘gnashing their teeth in suffering’ or ‘to of suffer so much as to gnash the teeth.’ As in the case of ⟦Acts 7:54|Acts 7:54⟧, it is important to avoid an expression for ‘gnashing the teeth’ which will suggest ‘gritting the teeth’ in the sense of determination or courageous resistance.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking
s.d: the grinding or the gnashing of the teeth, whether involuntary as in the case of certain illnesses, or as an expression of an emotion such as anger or of pain and suffering
s.g: to grind the teeth; to gnash the teeth; gnashing of teeth
s.c: In translating ‘they ground their teeth at him’ (⟦Acts 7:54|Acts 7:54⟧) it may be necessary to indicate the type of emotion which is involved in such an action, for example, ‘in anger they ground their teeth at him’ or ‘they showed their anger by grinding their teeth.’ It is essential to avoid an expression such as ‘to grit the teeth,’ which in English is a symbol of determination, not of anger.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to grind one’s teeth) to express and manifest intense anger
s.c: As noted in LN 23.41, it is possible to understand the expression βρύχω τοὺς ὀδόντας in both a literal as well as a figurative sense. The persons may very well have ‘ground their teeth’ as a sign of their anger and fury, so that a statement about what such persons did could be true in a literal as well as in a figurative sense.

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
s.d: to cause a forceful and abundant supply of a liquid
s.g: to cause to pour out; to cause to gush out
s.c: This flow from a spring may be referred to in some languages as ‘to cause to come out’ or ‘to cause to flow out.’

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
s.c: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as ⟦Matthew 6:11|Matthew 6:11⟧ as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering ⟦Luke 4:4|Luke 4:4⟧ (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of ⟦Luke 4:4|Luke 4:4⟧ is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: any type of solid food, particularly meat

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: (derivative of {L:βρῶσις<SDBG:βρῶσις:000000>}[a] ‘eating,’ {D:23.3}) pertaining to what can be eaten

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to consume solid food

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: a meal whether simple or elaborate
s.g: a meal; a banquet; a feast
s.c: Though ἄριστον, δεῖπνον, and βρῶσις are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of ⟦Mark 6:21|Mark 6:21⟧ that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
s.c: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as ⟦Matthew 6:11|Matthew 6:11⟧ as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. The meaning of ⟦Luke 4:4|Luke 4:4⟧ is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: any type of solid food, particularly meat

s.dp: Natural Substances › Metals
s.d: the process of producing rust or tarnish by oxidation{N:003}
s.c: Though in ⟦Matthew 6:19|Matthew 6:19⟧ βρῶσις has been generally understood to mean ‘corrosion,’ it might actually refer to a type of insect, as it does in the Septuagint of Malachi LN 3.11.

s.dp: Linear Movement › Come/Go Down, Descend
s.d: to cause to go down into water or other liquid substance

s.dp: Case › To Cause To Experience
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:βυθίζω<SDBG:βυθίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to cause to sink,’ {D:15.115}) to cause someone to experience serious consequences
s.g: to cause; to bring upon; to pull down to

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Bodies of Water
s.d: the relatively deep area of the sea or ocean sufficiently far from land as to be beyond the range of any protection from the seacoast
s.g: open sea; high sea; the deep; ocean
s.c: In order to designate the high sea or the ocean, it may be necessary in some instances to speak of ‘the sea far from land’ or ‘the sea out of sight of land.’ People who live near the ocean and are seafaring frequently have quite distinct terms for different conditions of the sea, whether, for example, it is stormy, moderately rough, or relatively calm. Languages may also use different terms in speaking of different areas of the sea or ocean. Note, for example, in English the use of China Sea, North Sea, Bering Sea, in contrast with Indian Ocean, Pacific Ocean, Atlantic Ocean. In English this contrast is relatively fixed, but it does reflect a gradation of size, since sea is used normally in speaking of smaller areas than is the case with ocean.

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: one who tans hides to make leather

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: (derivative of {L:βύσσος<SDBG:βύσσος:000000>} ‘fine linen,’ {D:6.166}) cloth consisting of fine linen

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: high quality cloth made from the stems of the flax plant; known for its strength and coolness{N:001}

s.dp: Artifacts › Furniture
s.d: an altar with a base or pedestal; for offering sacrifices to a god
s.c: In this only reference in the NT in which βωμός occurs, the altar to the Unknown God may be spoken of as ‘a place for offerings to a god whom people do not know’ or ‘… god whose name is not known.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the Aramaic name for a paved area outside the residence of Pontius Pilate and the setting for the public trial of Jesus; see {D:7.71}

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: an archangel

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: a disease involving severe inflammation and possibly a cancerous spread of ulcers which eat away the flesh and bones

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of Γάδαρα ‘Gadara,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who lives in or is a native of Gadara

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Treasure
s.d: a number of possessions and valuables constituting an important and official asset of a political entity

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city in southwest Palestine on a principal road to Egypt

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a room in the Temple used as a treasury
s.c: It is possible that in ⟦John 8:20|John 8:20⟧ γαζοφυλάκιον designates the offering boxes rather than the treasury itself (see γαζοφυλάκιον, LN 6.141). If one interprets γαζοφυλάκιον in ⟦John 8:20|John 8:20⟧ as the offering boxes, then one may translate ‘he spoke these words near where the offering boxes were.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Containers
s.d: a large box in which offerings were placed
s.c: The offering box in the Temple was also referred to as δῶρον (LN 6.142).

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Macedonian companion of Paul

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Christian from Derbe

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a man from Corinth who was baptized by Paul

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the recipient of 3 John

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: white fluid secreted by women and female mammals for nourishment of their young; also used as food for humans
s.c: The term γάλα may refer to any type of milk, whether produced by humans or by certain domesticated animals, for example, cow, sheep, goat, camel.|In a number of languages two distinct terms are used for milk, one identifying the human milk and another term specifying milk from animals. In the context of ⟦1 Corinthians 3:2|1 Corinthians 3:2⟧ it is probably the latter reference which is important, though the passage is highly figurative and the emphasis is upon food for babies.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Γαλατία<SDBG:Γαλατία:000000>} ‘Galatia,’ {D:93.442}) a person who is a native of Galatia

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a district in the Roman province of Asia

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Γαλατία<SDBG:Γαλατία:000000>} ‘Galatia,’ {D:93.442}) pertaining to Galatia

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
s.d: a calm or unruffled surface of a body of water
s.g: a calm (in contrast with a storm over water)
s.c: A calm after a storm may be referred to figuratively in some languages as ‘the water lay down’ or ‘the waves sank down again’ or ‘the water became like a table top.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a district in the northern part of Palestine

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the Lake of Galilee, also called Tiberias and Gennesaret

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Γαλιλαία<SDBG:Γαλιλαία:000000>} ‘Galilee,’ {D:93.444}) a person who is a native of Galilee

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Roman proconsul of Achaia

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a renowned Pharisee in Jerusalem

s.dp: Association › Marriage, Divorce
s.d: to enter into a marriage relation, applicable either to a man or to a woman{N:001}

s.dp: Association › Marriage, Divorce
s.d: to enter into a marriage relation, applicable either to a man or to a woman{N:001}
s.c: Some interpreters understand γαμίζω in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:38|1 Corinthians 7:38⟧ to mean ‘to give in marriage’ (see LN 34.72). See also the discussion at LN 13.32.

s.dp: Association › Marriage, Divorce
s.d: to cause a person to become married

s.dp: Association › Marriage, Divorce
s.d: the state of being married{N:001}

s.dp: Association › Marriage, Divorce
s.d: the ceremony associated with becoming married

s.dp: Constructions › Parts and Areas of Buildings
s.d: a relatively large room, often serving as a place for a wedding
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 22:10|Matthew 22:10⟧ a number of manuscripts read νυμφών rather than γάμος.

s.dp: Relations › Cause and/or Reason
s.d: a marker of cause or reason between events, though in some contexts the relation is often remote or tenuous

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Markers of Transition
s.d: a marker of a new sentence, but often best left untranslated or reflected in the use of ‘and’ or the conjunctive adverb ‘then.’
s.c: It is possible that in ⟦Matthew 27:23|Matthew 27:23⟧ the conjunction γάρ reflects Pilate’s attempt to reason with the crowd demanding Jesus’ crucifixion, but γάρ serves primarily to highlight the significance of the question rather than to provide a reason.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the inward parts of the body, either the digestive system (as in γαστέρες ἀργαί, literally ‘lazy bellies,’ but meaning ‘gluttons’ {S:05600101200026}) or the womb (in set phrases such as συλλαμβάνω ἐν γαστρί ‘to conceive’ {S:04200103100010}; ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχω ‘be pregnant’ {S:04000101800044} and elsewhere)
s.c: See also LN 23.19, LN 23.49, and LN 23.50.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γαστήρ<SDBG:γαστήρ:000000>}[a] ‘belly,’ {D:8.68}) a person who habitually eats excessively
s.c: A glutton is often spoken of idiomatically, for example, ‘a large belly’ or ‘a person who is only a stomach’ or ‘a professional eater.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to have in the womb) to be in a state of pregnancy
s.c: This expression contrasts with the meaning of συλλαμβάνω, LN 23.49, in that it seems to focus more upon the state of pregnancy rather than the event of conception.|It is impossible to determine whether in ⟦Matthew 1:23|Matthew 1:23⟧ (ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει καὶ τέξεται υἱόν ‘she will be pregnant and bear a son’) the focus is upon the state of pregnancy or the fact of conception (see LN 23.49).

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Markers of Emphasis
s.d: marker of relatively weak emphasis
s.c: This word is frequently not translated but possibly reflected in the word order.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a military leader and hero of Israel

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
s.d: a place of punishment for the dead
s.c: The Greek term γέεννα is derived from a Hebrew phrase meaning ‘Valley of Hinnom,’ a ravine running along the south side of Jerusalem and a place where the rubbish from the city was constantly being burned. According to late Jewish popular belief, the last judgment was to take place in this valley, and hence the figurative extension of meaning from ‘Valley of Hinnom’ to ‘hell.’ In most languages γέεννα is rendered as ‘place of punishment’ or ‘place where the dead suffer’ or ‘place where the dead suffer because of their sins.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: a person who lives close beside others and who thus by implication is a part of a so-called in-group, that is, the group with which an individual identifies both ethnically and culturally
s.c: It may be that of the three terms γείτων, περίοικος, the last is somewhat broader in meaning. At least πλησίον is used in ⟦Luke 10:27|Luke 10:27⟧ in a somewhat extended sense of ‘fellow man,’ while ἀδελφός probably suggests a more intimate or close relationship.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Laugh, Cry, Groan
s.c: A number of languages distinguish clearly between various types of laughter: (1) laughter directed against some person as a form of ridicule; (2) laughter resulting from seeing some humorous event or as the result of listening to a humorous account; and (3) laughter which reflects happiness and joy. In ⟦Luke 6:21|Luke 6:21⟧ and ⟦James 4:9|James 4:9⟧ it is this third type of laughter which is relevant to the contexts.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Laugh, Cry, Groan
s.c: A number of languages distinguish clearly between various types of laughter: (1) laughter directed against some person as a form of ridicule; (2) laughter resulting from seeing some humorous event or as the result of listening to a humorous account; and (3) laughter which reflects happiness and joy. In ⟦Luke 6:21|Luke 6:21⟧ and ⟦James 4:9|James 4:9⟧ it is this third type of laughter which is relevant to the contexts.

s.dp: Quantity › Full, Empty
s.d: to fill an object with a substance (normally used of masses)

s.dp: Quantity › Full, Empty
s.d: to be full of some substance or objects
s.g: to be full of; to contain
s.c: In ⟦Luke 11:39|Luke 11:39⟧ there is a mixed figure of speech, and as a result γέμω may be interpreted as indicating a degree of intensity.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › General
s.d: people living at the same time and belonging to the same reproductive age-class
s.g: those of the same time; those of the same generation
s.c: The expression ‘the people of this generation’ may also be expressed as ‘the people living now’ or ‘the people of this time.’ Successive generations may be spoken of as ‘groups of people who live one after the other’ or ‘successions of parents and children.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
s.d: an ethnic group exhibiting cultural similarities
s.c: Compare γενεά those of the same time (LN 11.4).

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: successive following generations of those who are biologically related to a reference person
s.c: In the case of γενεά, τέκνον, and σπέρμα (LN 10.29), the reference is not to one’s immediate descendants or offspring (that is to say, to one’s sons or daughters) but to a successive series of such persons, one’s descendants. In some languages such descendants may be called merely ‘the children of one’s children,’ and in other languages one may refer to descendants as ‘those who follow one’ or ‘those who come later.’

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: an indefinite period of time, but in close relationship to human existence and in some contexts, a period of time about the length of a generation
s.c: It is, of course, possible in ⟦Acts 14:16|Acts 14:16⟧ that the reference should be to ‘generations’ in the sense of periods of time.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: to have descended from a particular lineage
s.g: to be in the lineage of; to be descended from
s.c: The meaning of ⟦Hebrews 7:6|Hebrews 7:6⟧ may also be expressed as ‘they were not his forefathers.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: (derivative of γενεαλογέομαι ‘to be descended from,’ {D:10.25}) a list of direct descendants or ascendants

s.dp: Festivals
s.d: a celebration or a festivity marking the anniversary of someone’s birth

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: coming into existence by birth
s.c: A literal translation of ⟦Matthew 1:18|Matthew 1:18⟧ as ‘this is the way that Jesus Christ was born’ might be misleading, since it would imply a description of the actual process of his birth rather than an account of those circumstances and events which took place in connection with his birth. It may, therefore, be better to translate ⟦Matthew 1:18|Matthew 1:18⟧ as ‘this is what happened when Jesus Christ was born’ or ‘these things happened at the time of Jesus Christ’s birth.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: persons of successive generations who are related by birth
s.c: In biblical times the reckoning of a lineage was somewhat complex in view of certain distinctions between legal and biological relations. The focus of meaning in γένεσις, οἶκος, and πατριά is not, however, the list of ancestors, but the lineage of successively related persons to which the reference person belongs. Some scholars, however, interpret γένεσις in ⟦Matthew 1:1|Matthew 1:1⟧ as being part of what is essentially a title for the book of Matthew and thus would render the introductory phrase as ‘the book of the history of Jesus Christ’ (see γένεσις ‘history,’ LN 33.19).|In some languages a successive series of ancestors is called ‘the forefathers’ or ‘those to whom one looks back’ or ‘those who have gone ahead.’ In other languages a lineage is referred to as ‘a person’s root’ or ‘a man’s trunk’ (referring to the trunk of a tree).

s.dp: Communication › Discourse Types
s.d: an account of the origin and life of someone
s.c: For the most part, scholars understand the phrase βίβλος γενέσεως in ⟦Matthew 1:1|Matthew 1:1⟧ as referring to the list of ancestors which immediately follows. Therefore, βίβλος γενέσεως is more often interpreted as ‘the record of the ancestors’ or ‘the birth record of …’ (see LN 10.24).

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Exist
s.d: the state of existence
s.c: In ⟦James 1:23|James 1:23⟧ the term γένεσις is largely redundant, for the reference could only be to a person’s own face.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: coming into existence by birth
s.c: In some languages ‘from the time he was born’ may be best rendered as ‘from the time he was a small baby.’ One may also render this expression of time as ‘a man who had always been blind’ or ‘a man who had never been able to see.’

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: (derivative of {L:γίνομαι<SDBG:γίνομαι:000002>}[c] ‘to become,’ {D:13.48}) that which is a product or result of becoming
s.g: product; yield; what is produced by

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: (derivative of {L:γεννάω<SDBG:γεννάω:000001>}[b] ‘to give birth,’ {D:23.52}) that which has been produced or born of a living creature
s.c: In some languages it may be possible to translate this phrase in ⟦Matthew 3:7|Matthew 3:7⟧ more or less literally, for example, ‘the offspring of vipers,’ in which ‘vipers’ means poisonous snakes, but in other languages this would be impossible, and one must therefore use ‘little snakes.’ For another interpretation of γέννημα in ⟦Matthew 3:7|Matthew 3:7⟧, see LN 58.26.

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Class, Kind
s.d: a kind or class of persons, with the implication of possessing certain derived characteristics
s.g: son of; offspring of; child of; kind of; one who has the characteristics of; person of
s.c: For another interpretation of γέννημα in ⟦Matthew 3:7|Matthew 3:7⟧, see LN 23.53.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: the male role in causing the conception and birth of a child
s.g: to be the father of; to procreate; to beget

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: to give birth to a child{N:001}
s.c: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.|γεννάω also occurs together with ἐξ αἱμάτων (⟦John 1:13|John 1:13⟧) and ἐκ τῆς σαρκός (⟦John 3:6|John 3:6⟧) in reference to physical birth. In ⟦John 3:5|John 3:5⟧, γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος has likewise been interpreted by some scholars as referring to physical birth (compare ⟦John 3:6|John 3:6⟧), but others understand this as referring to baptism. Certainly the occurrence of γεννηθῇ with πνεύματος in ⟦John 3:5|John 3:5⟧ is a reference to religious rebirth, in which case γεννάω would involve a radical change of state (see LN 13.56). The use of the same word with two different meanings or referents is typical of the style of the Gospel of John.

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γεννάω<SDBG:γεννάω:000001>}[b] ‘to give birth,’ {D:23.52}) to cause to experience a radical change, with the implication of involvement of the total personality
s.g: to cause to be born; to be born of
s.c: The phrase γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος has been interpreted by some as a literal reference to physical birth (see LN 23.52). Others, however, interpret this phrase as referring to baptism by water. In a parallel fashion, the expression γεννηθῇ ἐξ … πνεύματος would refer to baptism by the Spirit or rebirth made possible by the Spirit.

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Happen
s.d: to cause to happen, with the implication of the result of existing circumstances
s.g: to cause; to produce; to give rise to

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Change Behavior
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be born again) to experience a complete change in one’s way of life to what it should be, with the implication of return to a former state or relation
s.g: to be born again; to experience new birth; rebirth
s.c: It is also possible to understand ἄνωθεν in ⟦John 3:3|John 3:3⟧ as meaning ‘from above’ or ‘from God’ (see LN 84.13), a literary parallel to the phrase ἐκ θεοῦ ἐγεννήθησαν in ⟦John 1:13|John 1:13⟧. In ⟦John 3:3|John 3:3⟧, however, Nicodemus understood ἄνωθεν as meaning ‘again’ (see LN 67.55) and γεννάω as ‘physical birth’ (see LN 23.52).

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a fertile plain south of Capernaum

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a name for the Lake of Galilee, also called the Lake of Tiberias

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: (derivative of {L:γεννάω<SDBG:γεννάω:000001>}[b] ‘to give birth,’ {D:23.52}) pertaining to having been born
s.g: one born; one who has been born; person
s.c: In some languages a literal rendering of γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν ‘born of women’ could be misleading, for it might suggest that there are persons who have not been born of women. It is for that reason that γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν may be rendered in some instances as ‘of all those persons who have ever lived.’ However, this reference to the preeminence of John the Baptist is difficult, and the implications of it go far beyond the matter of translational equivalence.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: a non-immediate descendant (possibly involving a gap of several generations), either male or female
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 22:16|Revelation 22:16⟧ ῥίζα (LN 10.33) and γένος are very similar in meaning, and it is often best to coalesce the two terms into a single expression, for example, ‘I am a descendant of David’ or ‘I belong to the lineage of David.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
s.d: a relatively large group of persons regarded as being biologically related{N:001}
s.c: It may be difficult in some languages to clearly distinguish between culture and race as in ⟦Mark 7:26|Mark 7:26⟧. Sometimes this difference can be indicated by saying ‘the woman lived like a Greek, but she was a Syrophoenician’ or ‘… her parents were from Syrophoenicia.’ In translating ‘people of my own race’ in ⟦Romans 11:14|Romans 11:14⟧, it may be necessary to say ‘all my fellow Jews’ or ‘all those people of whom I am a part’ or ‘those people who are my roots’ or ‘… my trunk,’ based on the analogy of a tree trunk and branches.

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Class, Kind
s.d: a category or class based upon an implied derivation and/or lineage

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of Γέρασα ‘Gerasa,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who lives in or is a native of Gerasa, a city in Peraea, east of the Jordan

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: the highest council of the Jews (see also {L:συνέδριον<SDBG:συνέδριον:000001>}[b] ‘Sanhedrin,’ the council of the Jews, {D:11.80}) but with the implication of the maturity and relative advanced age of those constituting the membership of such a council{N:001}
s.g: Sanhedrin; high council of the Jews

s.dp: People › Males
s.d: an adult male, with emphasis upon relatively advanced age

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Taste
Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to consume solid food

s.dp: Case › Experiencer
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γεύομαι<SDBG:γεύομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to taste,’ {D:24.72}) to experience, probably focusing on personal involvement

s.dp: Agriculture
s.d: to engage in agriculture or gardening
s.g: to cultivate land; to farm; to garden

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Pastures and Cultivated Lands
s.d: cultivated land, normally restricted to tilled fields or orchards, in contrast with pasture land (in the NT γεώργιον is used only figuratively of people whom God cares for and nurtures)

s.dp: Agriculture
s.d: (derivative of {L:γεωργέω<SDBG:γεωργέω:000000>} ‘to cultivate land,’ {D:43.1}) one who engages in agriculture or gardening

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › The Earth's Surface
s.d: the surface of the earth as the dwelling place of mankind, in contrast with the heavens above and the world below{N:001}

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Land in Contrast With the Sea
s.d: dry land, in contrast with the sea
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between terms which designate land in contrast with water and those which designate cultivated land. Even in English the normal term for land close to water is ‘shore’ or ‘coast,’ and therefore one may translate ⟦Matthew 14:24|Matthew 14:24⟧ as ‘the boat was already far away from the shore.’ Similarly, in ⟦Acts 27:27|Acts 27:27⟧ one may translate ‘we were getting close to shore.’

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: the loose top layer of earth in which plants grow, usually black, brown, or reddish in color and made of organic matter and mineral particles{N:002}
s.c: The meaning of γῆ may be expressed in some instances as soil for planting or ground for plants.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Sociopolitical Areas
s.d: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration{N:003}
s.g: region; territory; land (and even district, though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
s.c: The meanings of γῆ, χώρα, κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

s.dp: People › Human Beings
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:γῆ<SDBG:γῆ:000000>}[a] ‘earth,’ {D:1.39}) all people who dwell on the earth

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Universe, Creation
s.d: a more or less fixed phrase: the heavens and the earth, equivalent to a single lexical item: the totality of God’s creation
s.c: There may be certain complications involved in rendering ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ as ‘heaven and earth,’ since ‘heaven’ might be interpreted in some languages as referring only to the dwelling place of God himself. The referents in this passage are ‘the sky and the earth,’ in other words, all of physical existence, but not the dwelling place of God, for the latter would not be included in what is destined to pass away.

s.dp: Time › Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
s.d: the period of advanced age, normally of a person beyond his or her prime{N:001}

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: to become old in age (referring to living beings)
s.g: to grow old; to become old

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Exist
s.d: to come into existence
s.g: to be formed; to come to exist

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › State
s.d: to possess certain characteristics, with the implication of their having been acquired

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Change of State
s.d: to come to acquire or experience a state
s.c: In some languages there is no convenient lexical item meaning simply ‘to become,’ but in all instances there are certain paraphrastic expressions which may be employed, for example, ‘to arrive at being’ or ‘to cease being one thing and be another’ or ‘to change to be.’ One must, however, beware in the case of ⟦John 1:14|John 1:14⟧ not to employ some expression which would suggest that Christ had lost his divine nature in becoming a person or that he only appeared to be human (docetism).

s.dp: Be, Become, Exist, Happen › Happen
s.d: to happen, with the implication that what happens is different from a previous state{N:001}
s.g: to happen; to occur; to come to be

s.dp: Linear Movement › Move, Come/Go
s.d: to make a change of location in space (a highly generic meaning)
s.g: to move; to come; to go
s.c: Though the meaning of γίνομαι is often given as ‘to become,’ it is clear that in contexts such as ⟦Acts 25:15|Acts 25:15⟧ and ⟦Acts 27:7|Acts 27:7⟧ it would be impossible to render γίνομαι by traditional expressions such as ‘to become.’ In these contexts movement is clearly indicated, and therefore one must frequently employ an expression such as ‘to come to,’ ‘to arrive at,’ or even ‘to travel to.’

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Have, Possess, Property, Owner
s.d: to belong to someone{N:002}

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Behavior, Conduct
s.d: to exist and to conduct oneself, with the particular manner specified by the context{N:003}
s.g: to conduct oneself; to behave; conduct

s.dp: Existence in Space › Be in a Place
s.d: to be in a place, with the possible implication of having come to be in such a place

s.dp: Existence in Space › Be in a Place
s.d: to come to be in a place
s.g: to come to be; to appear; to be in a place

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Markers of Transition
s.d: a marker of new information, either concerning participants in an episode or concerning the episode itself (occurring normally in the formulas ἐγένετο δέ or καὶ ἐγένετο{N:004}
s.g: there was; and it happened that
s.c: Often left untranslated.

s.dp: Association › Marriage, Divorce
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to become to a man) to become married to a man

s.dp: Think › To Decide, To Conclude
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to become of a mind) to make up one’s mind, with emphasis upon the process of coming to such a decision{N:005}
s.g: to decide; to make up one’s mind

s.dp: Know
s.d: to possess information about
s.g: to know; to know about; to have knowledge of; to be acquainted with; acquaintance

s.dp: Learn
s.d: to acquire information by whatever means, but often with the implication of personal involvement or experience

s.dp: Learn
s.d: to learn to know a person through direct personal experience, implying a continuity of relationship
s.g: to know; to become acquainted with; to be familiar with
s.c: In translating γινώσκω in ⟦John 17:3|John 17:3⟧, it is important to avoid an expression which will mean merely ‘to learn about.’ Here the emphasis must be on the interpersonal relationship which is experienced.

s.dp: Understand › Come To Understand
s.d: to come to an understanding as the result of ability to experience and learn{N:002}
s.g: to come to understand; to perceive; to comprehend
s.c: It is also possible to interpret γινώσκω in ⟦Matthew 13:11|Matthew 13:11⟧ as meaning ‘to know about’ (see LN 28.1).

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Acknowledge
s.d: to indicate that one does know
s.c: It is also possible that in ⟦1 Corinthians 8:3|1 Corinthians 8:3⟧ γινώσκω means only ‘to know’ (LN 28.1).

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sexual Relations
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γινώσκω<SDBG:γινώσκω:000000>}[a] to know, {D:28.1})
s.c: In almost all languages there are euphemistic ways of speaking about sexual intercourse, and the use of γινώσκω and συνέρχομαι is illustrative of this in the Greek NT. It is possible to translate γινώσκω in ⟦Luke 1:34|Luke 1:34⟧ as simply for I am not married to a man, and likewise, συνέρχομαι in ⟦Matthew 1:18|Matthew 1:18⟧ may be rendered as ‘before they were married.’ In some languages one may use such expressions as ‘before they were joined’ or ‘before they slept together’ or ‘before they discovered one another.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Plant Products
s.d: a new, sweet wine in process of fermentation

s.dp: Features of Objects › Sweet, Bitter, Tasteless
s.d: pertaining to being sweet in contrast with being bitter or salty
s.c: In a number of languages it would be somewhat misleading to speak of ‘sweet water,’ since this would suggest water to which sugar or some other sweet substance had been added. The equivalent in ⟦James 3:11|James 3:11⟧ may be ‘fresh water’ or ‘good water’ in contrast with ‘bad water’ or ‘not bitter water’ in contrast with ‘bitter water.’
